Read the worked example before attempting the exercises. A quadratic equation is any equation that can be rearranged into the standard form ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero with a not equal to zero, and while some quadratics factor neatly over the integers, most do not, so you will need the quadratic formula or the method of completing the square, both of which are derived from the same underlying identity and both of which will give the same two roots whenever the discriminant is positive, the same repeated root when it is zero, and a pair of complex conjugates when it is negative, which is why the discriminant is worth computing first even when you intend to factor, since it tells you in one step whether factoring over the integers has any chance of succeeding and saves you the several minutes you would otherwise spend hunting for a pair of factors that was never going to exist, minutes that are far better spent checking the arithmetic of the substitution you are about to make into the formula, because a sign error there is by a wide margin the most common way of arriving at a confident and completely wrong pair of roots.
